newsitem.title: GREECE: Greek farmers block main highway with tractors.
newsitem.headline: Greek farmers block main highway with tractors.

text.p: Greek farmers, demanding higher prices and fuel subsidies, blocked the main north-south highway with thousands of tractors for a second day on Friday and said they would keep up their protest until their demands were met.

"This mockery must stop now," Yannis Pattakis, a farmers' union leader in the central town of Larissa told reporters. "This is a survival issue and we demand an immediate solution or we will stay here for as long as it takes."

The farmers, hard hit by low produce prices set by the European Union, have blocked the highway linking Athens with the northern port city of Salonika in Larissa and two other points with about 5,000 tractors, police said.
Traffic was being diverted via smaller back roads but it was difficult and slow, police said.
"We want a meeting with the prime minister (Costas Simitis) because we are tired of all the false promises by various ministers," Pattakis said.
Similar blockades in March last year cut the country in half for more than two weeks and ended after a personal plea by late socialist Prime Minister Andreas Papandreou.
The farmers held up traffic outside Larissa, many flying black flags throughout the night despite freezing temperatures.
Simitis turned down the request for a meeting, sending two ministers to Larissa to start negotiations with the protesters.
The farmers want a reduction of value added tax (VAT) for their tractors, lower prices for fertilisers, petrol and seeds.
They want higher higher prices for their products, especially cotton, and a settlement of the debts of the farmers' cooperatives with the state Agricultural Bank, amounting to $1.3 billion.
Agriculture Minister Stephanos Tzoumakas said the protests were politically motivated by the conservative and communist opposition parties.
The farmers' protests and angry reactions by labour unions against a tough 1997 budget, submitted in parliament on Friday, was the first test for Simitis' socialist government elected in September.
Greece came to a near halt on Thursday during a 24-hour general strike by thousands of workers disrupting transport, schools, hospitals and public services.
National Economy Minister Yannos Papandoniou said the budget would be the toughest in 15 years as Greece struggles to get its economy in line with its EU partners.
Simitis has said his priority is to join European economic and monetary union (EMU) by 2001, two years after the main core of EU states plans to launch the Euro single European currency.
Papandoniou has vowed to tax the wealthy hard but he has rejected numerous requests from organised labour to ease the economic hardship of lower salaried workers.
"This government feels for the problems of the workers, and especially the weaker social strata and asks for understanding," a government statement said on Thursday.
